The Slow Death of the Hyperlink

By A. Writer

There was a time when the web pointed outward. Every page was a doorway, and following links was how you found the next thing worth reading. Writers linked generously because linking was the point: a page was a node in a conversation that spanned thousands of sites, and the act of pointing elsewhere was a form of respect.

Somewhere along the way the doors started closing. Platforms discovered that every outbound link was a user walking out the door, and they began, slowly and then quickly, to discourage them. Links were demoted in feeds, hidden behind interstitials, stripped from posts, and finally treated as a kind of spam.

The consequences were subtle at first. Search got worse because the signal it relied on — people vouching for other pages by linking to them — thinned out. Blogs, which lived on links, quietly lost their audiences. The open web did not die so much as it stopped being walked.

What we lost was not just traffic but a habit of mind. Following a link is an act of curiosity; it says the thing in front of you is not the whole story. A web without links is a web of dead ends, each one optimised to keep you exactly where you are.

There are reasons for hope. Newsletters link freely again. Personal sites are having a quiet revival. Tools for saving and revisiting the things we find are better than they have ever been. The hyperlink is not dead. It is waiting for us to use it.
